title: Year four close
hook: next year: reading the Granth yourself, and living it

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world. Your line was what I think now. Did you write your sentence down, with the date beside it? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-six.

A bookmark sits in a book like a small promise. It says: someone was here, and someone is coming back. All year, this path has been reading around a book. Lines quoted from it, hymns sung from it, a code built around it, people bowing before it in places all over the map. But mostly the book has come to you in pieces, a line at a time, in paraphrase. Today year four closes. Tomorrow the bookmark moves, and the path puts the Granth itself into your hands.
screen: `A BOOKMARK IS A SMALL PROMISE.` → `A YEAR AROUND ONE BOOK.` → `NEXT, THE BOOK ITSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the year in one breath. It was called the ways of the Guru. It began with the ragas, the musical moods in which the Granth's hymns are arranged. Then Guru Nanak's longer teachings: the dialogue with the yogis, the poem on the alphabet's letters, the song of the months. Then the Gurus who followed him, and the Ninth Guru's calm. Then the writings of the Tenth Guru. Then the Khalsa and the shared code. Then the living streams of the panth and its places. And last, Sikh thought. Second, notice what sat at the center of every block. The ragas are the Granth's own order. The Gurus' teachings are its hymns. The code is built around it, and the streams bow before it. Even the thought came to us as its lines. All year, the Granth was the hub, and we stood a little way off, describing it. Third, here's what changes. Year five is called the Granth itself, and living it. It starts small: how to read a page. The small signs on the letters, what a hymn's heading tells you, where a hymn's center line sits. Then it walks through the Granth in order, from its opening pages to its closing ones, a reading a day. Not the whole text; a guided walk. And then it turns to living it, through a whole life. Fourth, a picture from near the Granth's close to carry over the threshold. In the Mundavani, Guru Arjan describes the book as a platter. In paraphrase: on this platter lie three things, truth, contentment and reflection, and the nectar of the Name is placed there too. Whoever eats it, whoever savors it, is set free. Next year, the platter is set down in front of you.
screen: `A YEAR CALLED THE WAYS OF THE GURU.` · `THE GRANTH AT THE CENTER OF IT ALL.` · `NEXT: READ A PAGE, THEN WALK IN ORDER.` · `THE MUNDAVANI'S PLATTER.` · then, large: `NEXT, THE GRANTH ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open the Granth, or plan to. Settle, and breathe. If you have a gutka, a printed copy, or a trusted app, open it to the first page. Don't try to read it yet. Just look. The shapes of the letters, the lines, the space around them. Let your eyes rest there. If you don't have one near you, plan instead: where you'll read, at what hour, from what copy. See yourself sitting down to it. If you pray, you can ask to come to it ready. The bell holds the time.
Year four close. The ways of the Guru, gathered up, and a turn toward the book at the center of them all. Today's word.
Your line: next, the granth itself. Today, choose where you'll read from, a gutka, a printed copy or a trusted app, and set it where you'll see it tomorrow. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs read the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara, at home from a gutka of daily prayers or a full copy, and also from printed or digital editions with Gurmukhi and translation side by side.
